demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Sameer describes his life now as being lived behind a thick pane of glass. He can see everything happening-his wife, Priya, asking about his day; the dispatcher's voice crackling over the radio; the blur of houses on his delivery route-but he feels disconnected from it all, the sounds muffled and the colors muted. He functions, he works, he eats, but the man who does these things is a stranger to him.

Nine months ago, he loved his job. There was a simple satisfaction in it. He knew the city's arteries and capillaries by heart, the rhythm of the traffic lights, the shortcuts that shaved minutes off a run. He was good at it-efficient, reliable, a familiar, friendly face to the people on his route. He and Priya were saving for a down payment on a small house, a place with a yard. The future felt solid, something he was building, one delivered package at a time.

The day it happened was unremarkable. Overcast, a steady November drizzle that slicked the roads. He was on his last run, heading down a residential street he'd driven a thousand times. He remembers the song on the radio, the rhythmic thump of the windshield wipers. Then, a flash of red from between two parked cars. He slammed on the brakes, the heavy van groaning as the tires screamed against the wet asphalt. The thud was sickeningly soft.

In the seconds that followed, the world went silent. All he could see was a small red jacket and a bicycle twisted on the pavement. He doesn't remember getting out of the van, only standing over the child, a boy of about eight, his own son's age. The boy was conscious, crying, but his leg was bent at an angle that defied nature.

The official investigation cleared him. He wasn't speeding, he wasn't on his phone. It was an accident, a terrible, unavoidable accident. The boy's parents, in a state of shock and grief, never pressed charges. The child survived, after multiple surgeries. Sameer knows these facts intellectually, but they provide no comfort. They are just words. The truth, for him, lives in the memory of that soft thud and the image of the red jacket.

That image appears without warning now. It will flash in his mind while he's handing a package to a customer, causing him to flinch. He sees it in his sleep, replaying the moment in agonizing slow motion, except in his dreams, he never hits the brakes in time. He wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart hammering against his ribs, the sound of Priya's gentle breathing beside him feeling like an accusation.

Driving, the skill that was once his pride, is now a daily exercise in terror. His knuckles are perpetually white from gripping the steering wheel. Every child on a scooter, every ball that rolls into the street, sends a surge of adrenaline through him so powerful it makes him dizzy. He scans the sidewalks with a frantic intensity, his body coiled and ready for a disaster that has already happened. He takes long, inefficient detours to avoid the street where the accident occurred. The sight of a red jacket on a child can make him pull over, unable to breathe.

At home, he is a ghost. Priya tries to reach him, her touch a question he can no longer answer. He sees the worry in her eyes but cannot offer her reassurance because he feels none himself. He snaps at her over small things-a dish left in the sink, the volume on the television. The anger feels safer than the immense, crushing weight of his guilt. He believes, in a place deeper than logic, that he is a monster. A careless person who ruined a child's life. The fact that he was legally absolved only makes it worse; there is no official punishment, so he carries out the sentence on himself, every minute of every day.
